introduction-decoupling-with-messages.core: Queues and topics decouple services in time and load. SQS buffers messages so consumers process at their own pace (point-to-point); SNS pushes each message to all subscribers (pub/sub). Together they absorb spikes, isolate failures and let systems scale independently.

first_principles.problem: A traffic spike overwhelms a downstream service called synchronously, and failures cascade upstream.
truths: Producers and consumers run at different speeds.

analogy.title: A restaurant ticket rail
analogy.story: Waiters pin orders; cooks take them when ready, and a rush doesn't crash the kitchen.
analogy.breaks: Tickets are taken by one cook; SNS gives every subscriber its own copy.

example.title: Absorbing a spike
flow: Backlog drains in minutes, nothing lost

check.q: What's the core difference between SQS and SNS?
check.a: SQS is a pull-based queue where each message goes to one consumer; SNS pushes each message to all subscribers.

sqs-standard-vs-fifo-speed-vs-order.core: Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing via deduplication within 5 minutes, with throughput limits (up to 300 msg/s per API action, 3,000 with batching, higher in high-throughput mode).

first_principles.problem: Bank ledger updates processed out of order corrupt balances.
truths: Ordering often matters only per entity.
derivation: **MessageGroupId** per entity (account) for parallel ordered streams.

analogy.title: A crowd entering a stadium versus a single-file queue per ticket desk
analogy.story: The crowd is fast but unordered; each desk keeps strict order.
analogy.breaks: Desks serve different people; message groups must be chosen to match ordering needs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each account ordered; accounts processed in parallel.

check.q: How does FIFO keep parallelism while preserving order?
check.a: Ordering is per MessageGroupId, so different groups are processed in parallel.

the-fan-out-pattern-sns-sqs.core: Fan-out publishes once to an SNS topic subscribed by several SQS queues, giving each consumer its own durable buffer, retries and pace. Subscription filter policies route only relevant messages to each queue, and raw message delivery avoids SNS wrapping.

first_principles.problem: Three services need every order event, but one slow consumer shouldn't affect the others.
truths: Not every consumer needs every message.

analogy.title: A newsletter delivered to separate mailboxes
analogy.story: Each subscriber reads at their own pace from their own box.
analogy.breaks: Mailboxes don't retry; SQS consumers retry and use DLQs independently.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: EU fulfilment queue receives only EU orders.

check.q: Why put an SQS queue behind each SNS subscriber?
check.a: It gives each consumer durable buffering, retries and independent pace, isolating slow or failing consumers.

visibility-timeout-preventing-double-wor.core: When a consumer receives a message, SQS hides it for the visibility timeout. If the consumer deletes it in time, it's done; if not (crash or slow), it reappears for another consumer. Set the timeout above the worst-case processing time (≥ 6× Lambda timeout for ESM), and extend it for long jobs.

first_principles.problem: Long jobs exceed the 30-second default, so messages reappear and are processed twice.
truths: Crashed consumers must not lose messages.

analogy.title: Checking out a library book
analogy.story: While it's on loan nobody else sees it; if you don't return it by the due date, it goes back on the shelf.
analogy.breaks: Library books can be renewed indefinitely; visibility can extend up to 12 hours max.

example.title: Extending visibility

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No duplicate processing of long jobs.

code.text:
msg = sqs.receive_message(QueueUrl=q, VisibilityTimeout=120)['Messages'][0]
# halfway through a long job:
sqs.change_message_visibility(QueueUrl=q, ReceiptHandle=msg['ReceiptHandle'], VisibilityTimeout=300)
process(msg)
sqs.delete_message(QueueUrl=q, ReceiptHandle=msg['ReceiptHandle'])

example.outcome: each message handled once in normal operation.

check.q: What happens if a consumer crashes before deleting a message?
check.a: After the visibility timeout expires, the message becomes visible again for another consumer.

dead-letter-queues-dlq-the-graveyard.core: A DLQ receives messages that failed processing maxReceiveCount times (redrive policy). It stops poison messages from looping forever, preserves them for inspection, and supports redrive back to the source queue after a fix. Always alarm on DLQ depth.

first_principles.problem: A malformed message fails forever, consuming capacity and hiding other issues.
truths: Some messages will never succeed without a fix.
derivation: Create a **DLQ** (same type: FIFO for FIFO).

analogy.title: A hospital's isolation ward
analogy.story: Patients who don't respond to standard treatment are moved aside for specialist attention.
analogy.breaks: Patients recover on their own sometimes; DLQ messages wait until someone acts.

check.q: Why set DLQ retention longer than the source queue's?
check.a: The message's original enqueue timestamp is kept, so it could expire soon after arriving in the DLQ.

sqs-long-polling-vs-short-polling.core: Short polling returns immediately, even with no messages, sampling a subset of servers, which wastes requests and money and can miss messages. Long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20) waits until messages arrive or the timeout elapses and queries all servers, reducing empty responses, cost and latency.

first_principles.problem: A consumer polls an idle queue in a tight loop, generating millions of empty requests per day.

analogy.title: Checking the post every second versus waiting by the letterbox
analogy.story: Waiting means you know immediately when post arrives, without endless trips.
analogy.breaks: Waiting by the letterbox ties you up; long polling releases after at most 20 s.
